steps.say: The ductus is meant to close, but prematurity keeps it open. Immature ductal muscle constricts poorly in oxygen, so the vessel that should seal in hours stays widely patent for days. In extremely low birth weight infants under 1000 grams, a haemodynamically significant PDA keeps troubling 50 to 70 percent of babies.
steps.tx: In **extremely low birth weight** infants under **1000 g**, the **preterm PDA incidence** of haemodynamically significant **patent ductus arteriosus** reaches **50-70%** of neonates. Immature ductal smooth muscle responds weakly to oxygen, while respiratory distress and fluids keep the shunt open. The result is pulmonary overcirculation with systemic steal exactly when fragile organs can least afford it.

steps.say: An open ductus keeps stealing from the body to flood the lungs. Blood runs off from the high pressure aorta into the low pressure pulmonary circulation throughout diastole, so diastolic pressure sags while systolic pressure holds. The gap between them is the wide pulse pressure felt as bounding water hammer pulses.
steps.tx: **Diastolic run-off** from the high pressure aorta into the low pressure **pulmonary circulation** lowers diastolic pressure and widens the **pulse pressure**. Clinicians feel **bounding peripheral pulses** with a collapsing water hammer character at the wrist. The same steal robs the gut, kidneys, and brain while the lungs drown in recirculated flow.

steps.say: No other murmur keeps behaving quite like this one. The classic Gibson murmur is continuous, rough, and machinery like, peaking around the second heart sound at the left infraclavicular area and second left intercostal space. It never fully disappears in systole or diastole, with the aortic to pulmonary gradient persisting throughout.
steps.tx: The classic **Gibson murmur** is the **continuous machinery murmur** of PDA: rough and machinery like, peaking around **S2**, best heard at the **left infraclavicular area** and **second left intercostal space**. Flow persists through systole and diastole because aortic pressure exceeds pulmonary pressure throughout the cycle. A thrill with bounding pulses and an active precordium completes the bedside picture.

steps.say: Not every PDA is obvious on listening. A term infant may carry only a soft continuous murmur with normal growth, while a preterm baby shows apnoeas, ventilator dependence, and feed intolerance. Maternal first trimester rubella classically pairs a persistent ductus with peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis, leaving deafness and cataracts as clues.
steps.tx: Term infants often show only a soft continuous murmur, but preterm babies develop **apnoea**, **ventilator dependence**, and **feed intolerance** from the steal. **Congenital rubella syndrome** after **maternal first trimester rubella** classically pairs persistent **patent ductus arteriosus** with **peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis**, leaving deafness and cataracts as clues. Deafness and cataracts in the same child should prompt a search for both lesions.

steps.say: Prostaglandins hold the ductus open, so blocking them closes it. Most units favour cyclooxygenase inhibitors first line in preterm infants, reserving surgery for failures. Dosing uses indomethacin at one fifth of a milligram per kilogram, ibuprofen at 10 milligrams per kilogram first then 5, or paracetamol at 15 milligrams per kilogram every 6 hours, watching renal function closely.
steps.tx: The **pharmacological closure drugs** are **cyclooxygenase inhibitors** that close the preterm ductus: **indomethacin 0.2 mg/kg**, **ibuprofen 10 mg/kg** first dose then **5 mg/kg**, or **paracetamol 15 mg/kg every 6 hours**. Treatment works best in the first two weeks while the ductus still reacts. Renal function, platelets, and gut perfusion are watched because all three drugs trade closure against organ ischaemia.

steps.say: When the kidneys or gut look vulnerable, drug choice matters. Ibuprofen matches indomethacin for closure success while carrying a clearly lower risk of necrotising enterocolitis and renal impairment. That safety margin has made ibuprofen the usual first pick in most neonatal units today.
steps.tx: The **ibuprofen safety profile** shows equal closure efficacy to **indomethacin** with significantly lower risk of **necrotizing enterocolitis** and **renal impairment**. Oliguria, rising creatinine, bleeding, and suspected gut ischaemia therefore favour ibuprofen or paracetamol. Indomethacin stays reserved for units and protocols built around it, with the same surveillance in place.

points: Higher gut and kidney injury risk
left.title: Indomethacin

steps.say: Left alone, a large ductus remodels the lung vessels until the shunt turns around. Severe pulmonary hypertension reverses PDA flow to right to left, producing differential cyanosis with blue lower limbs and clubbed toes but a pink normal upper body. Closure after reversal is forbidden because the duct is then the only outlet.
steps.tx: When **severe pulmonary hypertension** reverses the shunt right to left, **differential cyanosis** appears: cyanosis of the **lower limbs** with pink normal **upper extremities**. The arch vessels arise proximal to the ductus and stay oxygenated while ductal blood desaturates the descending aorta. Reversed flow marks inoperability, so oxygen in the feet is always compared with the right hand.

vis.alt: Diagrams show pink oxygenated upper body and cyanotic lower body from a reversed ductal shunt.
vis.caption: Eisenmenger ductal shunt causing pink top and blue lower body. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.say: Drugs cannot close every ductus, with term vessels responding barely to them. Percutaneous transcatheter closure with coils or duct occluders is the standard treatment for term infants and older children weighing above 5 to 6 kilograms. Surgical ligation remains the backup when drugs fail, are contraindicated, or the baby is too small for a device.
steps.tx: **Transcatheter coil and occluder** closure is standard for term infants and older children above **5-6 kg**, with same day mobilisation and no chest scar. Ductal anatomy on angiography chooses coil against occluder, and significant residual flow earns reintervention. **Surgical ligation** stays the backup for failed or contraindicated drugs and for tiny infants below device size.
